content.content:
1	# ChronicleFlow
2	
3	ChronicleFlow is a small backend for durable workflow orchestration. It stores
4	workflow definitions, execution state, and an append-only event history in
5	SQLite so an execution can be inspected and replayed deterministically.
6	
7	The initial release intentionally supports a compact public contract:
8	
9	- workflows are directed acyclic graphs of `task`, `condition`, and bounded
10	  `loop` nodes;
11	- executions advance one ready task at a time, evaluating conditions and
12	  skipping unmatched branches automatically;
13	- task nodes may declare a bounded number of retries: a submitted failure
14	  re-queues the node until the retries are exhausted, which terminates the
15	  execution;
16	- a task node may declare an approval point with the people allowed to decide
17	  it; advancing parks the task in a waiting state until an approver approves
18	  (completing it with the submitted output) or rejects (terminating the
19	  execution with reason `rejected`);
20	- executions may declare a timeout in seconds, after which they terminate and
21	  no longer accept output, and they may be cancelled explicitly;
22	- loop nodes repeat their body a bounded number of times, re-evaluating a
23	  continue condition at the loop boundaries;
24	- every state transition is appended to the execution event stream;
25	- replay rebuilds execution state from the recorded events;
26	- a checkpoint is written at every node boundary, capturing the state
27	  summary and event position, so an execution can be recovered from the
28	  latest checkpoint after a restart;
29	- workers may claim a running execution to receive a work item with a
30	  time-bounded lease, renew the lease with heartbeats, and release it;
31	  while a lease is active only its holder may submit results, and an
32	  expired or released lease returns the work item to the claimable set;
33	- duplicate commands with the same idempotency key return the original result;
34	- workflows and executions may declare webhook subscriptions, and matching
35	  business events are delivered to the declared targets with bounded retries,
36	  each delivery recorded in a per-execution history;
37	- a workflow may declare a schedule — a fixed interval in seconds or a
38	  five-field cron plan — and the service automatically creates one execution
39	  per due period with the declared input; schedules can be paused and
40	  resumed, and periods missed while paused are either caught up once or
41	  skipped, according to the declared missed policy.
42	
43	## Requirements
44	
45	- Python 3.11 or newer
46	- no third-party runtime dependencies
47	
48	## Run the service
49	
50	```bash
51	PYTHONPATH=src python -m chronicleflow.server --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --database chronicleflow.db
52	```
53	
54	The process prints `ChronicleFlow listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080` after it
55	has bound the port.
56	
57	## HTTP API
58	
59	All request and response bodies are JSON. Unknown fields are rejected.
60	
61	### Tenants and quotas
62	
63	A request may declare a tenant by sending the `X-Tenant-Id` header with a
64	non-empty identifier. Every workflow, execution, schedule, schedule status,
65	and delivery history record is scoped to the tenant of the request that
66	created it: queries and operations only ever see data belonging to that
67	tenant, and different tenants may use the same workflow or execution
68	identifiers without colliding. Referencing another tenant's resource — for
69	example advancing, deciding, claiming, cancelling, recovering, replaying, or
70	reading the events, checkpoints, deliveries, or schedule of an execution or
71	workflow owned by another tenant — is answered exactly like a reference to a
72	missing resource: `404 not_found`, with no indication that the resource
73	exists elsewhere. An execution created in one tenant can only reference a
74	workflow of the same tenant; referencing an unseen workflow identifier is the
75	usual `404 not_found`.
76	
77	The header applies to every workflow, execution, and schedule entry point,
78	including creation, advancement, approval decisions, lease operations,
79	cancellation, recovery, replay, and all history and status queries. An empty
80	`X-Tenant-Id` value is a `400 validation_error`. Requests that omit the
81	header entirely keep using the single legacy namespace, whose advancement,
82	approvals, leases, retries, timeouts, cancellation, checkpoints, recovery,
83	scheduling, and replay behavior is byte-for-byte unchanged: the tenant is
84	stored only as database scope, never added to a state field or event payload,
85	and state shapes and event streams gain no new fields. Idempotency keys are
86	scoped per tenant as well, so tenants can never see or collide with each
87	other's keys; reusing a key for another operation within the same tenant is
88	the usual `409 conflict`.
89	
90	A tenant may declare quotas bounding how many workflows and executions it may
91	hold:
92	
93	```http
94	PUT /quotas
95	Idempotency-Key: quota-request-1
96	X-Tenant-Id: acme
97	
98	{"workflows": 10, "executions": 100}
99	```
100	
101	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body must contain exactly
102	`workflows` and `executions`, each a positive integer; a non-positive,
103	non-integer, boolean, or non-finite value, a missing or extra field, or a
104	non-object body is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing. Both quota
105	routes require a tenant: calling them without `X-Tenant-Id` (or with an empty
106	one) is a `400 validation_error`. The response is
107	`{"quota":{"workflows":10,"executions":100}}`; declaring again replaces the
108	limits (re-anchoring nothing else). Lowering a limit below the current
109	holding deletes no existing data — existing workflows and executions stay
110	fully usable — it only rejects later writes that would exceed the new limit.
111	
112	```http
113	GET /quotas
114	X-Tenant-Id: acme
115	```
116	
117	Returns the declared quota, or the definite empty result `{"quota":null}`
118	when the tenant has declared none.
119	
120	When a write would take the tenant past either limit, the whole request is
121	rejected with `409 conflict` and an error message that names the quota (for
122	example `quota exceeded: tenant already holds 10 workflows (quota limit is
123	10)`), so callers can tell quota rejection apart from an ordinary identifier
124	conflict. The rejection performs no partial write: nothing is inserted and
125	previously stored data is unaffected, exactly as for validation failures.
126	
127	A schedule firing on time creates its execution in the schedule's tenant and
128	that execution counts against the tenant's execution quota. When the tenant
129	is at its execution limit, the due period creates no execution and the
130	schedule is left unchanged — its cursor, `last_triggered_at`, and
131	`last_execution_id` stay as they were — so the period is settled on a later
132	pass once capacity exists, under the usual per-period idempotence. Delivery
133	history follows the tenant of the execution it belongs to.
134	
135	### Health
136	
137	```http
138	GET /health
139	```
140	
141	Returns `{"status":"ok"}`.
142	
143	### Create a workflow
144	
145	```http
146	POST /workflows
147	Idempotency-Key: workflow-request-1
148	
149	{
150	  "id": "order-flow",
151	  "nodes": [
152	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
153	    {"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
154	  ]
155	}
156	```
157	
158	Returns HTTP 201 with the stored workflow. Node identifiers must be unique,
159	dependencies must exist, and cycles are rejected.
160	
161	A workflow may also declare webhook `subscriptions` alongside its nodes:
162	
163	```json
164	{
165	  "id": "order-flow",
166	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
167	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/orders", "events": ["execution_completed"]}]
168	}
169	```
170	
171	See "Webhook notifications" below for the subscription shape and delivery
172	semantics; the subscriptions apply to every execution of the workflow.
173	
174	A workflow may also declare a `schedule` alongside its nodes:
175	
176	```json
177	{
178	  "id": "nightly-orders",
179	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
180	  "schedule": {"interval_seconds": 3600, "input": {"mode": "nightly"}, "missed_policy": "catch_up"}
181	}
182	```
183	
184	See "Schedules" below for the declaration shape and the trigger semantics.
185	
186	Besides `task`, a node may have `kind` set to `condition`:
187	
188	```json
189	{"id": "is_vip", "kind": "condition", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "path": "customer.vip", "equals": true}
190	```
191	
192	`path` is a non-empty dot-separated path into the execution input and `equals`
193	is a JSON scalar (string, number, boolean, or null). A condition is evaluated
194	automatically once its dependencies complete: the input value at `path` is
195	compared with `equals` by JSON type and value, and a missing path evaluates to
196	`false`.
197	
198	A task may carry an optional `run_if` guard:
199	
200	```json
201	{"id": "expedite", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["is_vip"], "run_if": {"condition_id": "is_vip", "expected": true}}
202	```
203	
204	`condition_id` must reference a `condition` node that is also listed in the
205	task's `depends_on`. When the condition's result differs from `expected`, the
206	task is marked as skipped: it receives no output and still satisfies the
207	dependencies of its successors.
208	
209	A task may declare how many times it is retried after a failure:
210	
211	```json
212	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "retries": 3}
213	```
214	
215	`retries` is an integer between 0 and 10 and defaults to 0, meaning the task
216	is attempted only once. Each failure submitted through `advance` consumes one
217	attempt; while retries remain, the task returns to the ready set and is
218	advanced again. When a failure arrives with no retries left, the task is
219	permanently failed and the whole execution terminates with termination reason
220	`retries_exhausted`.
221	
222	A task may instead declare an approval point:
223	
224	```json
225	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "approval": {"approvers": ["alice", "bob"]}}
226	```
227	
228	`approval` contains exactly `approvers`, a non-empty array of approver
229	identifier strings without duplicates; an empty list, a duplicate entry, or a
230	non-string entry is a validation error, and only `task` nodes may carry an
231	approval point. When an `advance` reaches a ready task with an approval point,
232	the task does not complete and the submitted output or failure is not
233	consumed: an `approval_requested` event is appended (recording the node, its
234	approvers, and, inside a loop body, the loop id and iteration) and the
235	execution stays `running`, parked in a waiting state returned under
236	`waiting_approval`. Further `advance` calls return the current state without
237	writing output, completing the node, or appending events; only a decision can
238	move the task.
239	
240	### Submit an approval decision
241	
242	```http
243	POST /executions/run-1/decision
244	Idempotency-Key: decision-request-1
245	
246	{"approver":"alice","decision":"approved","output":{"charge_id":"c-3"}}
247	```
248	
249	`decision` is either `approved` or `rejected`. An approved decision carries
250	exactly `approver`, `decision`, and an `output` object; the task completes with
251	that output and its successors become available in the usual way. A rejected
252	decision carries exactly `approver`, `decision`, and a `reason` string; the
253	task is permanently failed (it is listed under `failed_nodes`) and the
254	execution terminates with termination reason `rejected`. Either decision
255	appends an `approval_decided` event with the node, approver, decision, and (on
256	rejection) the reason, and the approval record is kept under `approvals`. A
257	request whose approver is not in the point's approver list is a 409
258	`conflict`, and a malformed body or a decision value other than `approved` or
259	`rejected` is a 400 `validation_error`; neither changes execution state.
260	Repeating the decision that already resolved the most recent approval point —
261	the same approver and decision with the same output or rejection reason —
262	returns the first result and neither advances the node again nor appends
263	another event; any other decision against an execution with no pending
264	approval point is a 409 `conflict`, and deciding a missing execution returns
265	404.
266	
267	While an execution is parked at an approval point it remains `running`, so a
268	cancellation takes effect immediately with the usual `cancelled` termination
269	reason, and a reached timeout terminates it with `timeout`; both dismiss the
270	pending point and the execution then no longer accepts decisions or output.
271	The waiting point, its request and decision events, and the termination
272	reason are rebuilt solely from the event stream on replay, and the parked and
273	decided node boundaries are checkpointed like every other boundary, so
274	waiting points and recorded decisions remain valid after a restart. Approval
275	state is added to an execution only when its workflow declares at least one
276	approval point; workflows without approvals keep exactly the previous state
277	shape and event stream.
278	
279	A node may also have `kind` set to `loop`, describing a bounded repeated
280	segment:
281	
282	```json
283	{"id": "retry", "kind": "loop", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "entry": "attempt", "condition": "keep_trying", "max_iterations": 3}
284	```
285	
286	A loop node contains exactly `id`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `entry`, `condition`,
287	and `max_iterations`; any other field is rejected as unknown. `entry` names a
288	`task` node, `condition` names a `condition` node, and `max_iterations` is an
289	integer between 1 and 100. The loop body is the entry task plus every node
290	reachable from it through `depends_on`; the body keeps the usual DAG rules and
291	must contain the referenced condition. The loop's own dependencies must be
292	completed or skipped before the first iteration may start, they must not
293	overlap the body, bodies of different loops must not overlap or nest, and
294	nodes outside a body must not depend on nodes inside it (they depend on the
295	loop node instead).
296	
297	When the loop's dependencies are satisfied, the loop evaluates its condition
298	against the execution input (same JSON type and value comparison as condition
299	nodes; a missing path is `false`). If it is `false`, the loop completes with
300	zero iterations and end reason `condition_false`. If it is `true`, the first
301	iteration starts and the body advances one ready task per `advance` call in
302	the usual deterministic order; conditions and `run_if` skips inside the body
303	are re-evaluated every iteration, and task outputs belong only to the current
304	iteration. Once every body node is completed or skipped, the condition is
305	evaluated again: `true` starts the next iteration, `false` ends the loop with
306	`condition_false`, and reaching `max_iterations` ends it with
307	`iteration_limit` after that iteration finishes. Ending the loop completes
308	the loop node and releases the dependencies of its successors.
309	
310	Execution state exposes each loop under `loops`: `status`, the
311	`current_iteration`, one entry per iteration with its own `completed_nodes`,
312	`skipped_nodes`, `condition_results`, and `outputs`, and the single
313	`end_reason` (`condition_false` or `iteration_limit`). The event stream
314	records `iteration_started`, `loop_condition_evaluated`, and `loop_completed`
315	events alongside the usual per-node ones, so replay rebuilds loop state
316	exactly.
317	
318	### Start an execution
319	
320	```http
321	POST /executions
322	Idempotency-Key: execution-request-1
323	
324	{"id":"run-1","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{"order_id":"o-7"}}
325	```
326	
327	Returns HTTP 201. The execution starts in `running` state.
328	
329	An execution may declare a timeout:
330	
331	```json
332	{"id":"run-2","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{},"timeout_seconds":30}
333	```
334	
335	`timeout_seconds` is a positive number of seconds counted from the moment the
336	execution starts. Once the deadline passes, the execution terminates with
337	termination reason `timeout` and no longer accepts output. Executions without
338	a timeout never expire.
339	
340	An execution may also declare its own webhook `subscriptions`, which apply in
341	addition to the ones its workflow declares:
342	
343	```json
344	{
345	  "id": "run-3",
346	  "workflow_id": "order-flow",
347	  "input": {},
348	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/ops", "events": ["node_completed"], "max_attempts": 3}]
349	}
350	```
351	
352	### Inspect an execution
353	
354	```http
355	GET /executions/run-1
356	GET /executions/run-1/events
357	GET /executions/run-1/checkpoints
358	```
359	
360	The first endpoint returns the materialized state. The second returns the
361	ordered event stream. The third returns the ordered checkpoints; each entry
362	gives its `sequence`, the `event_sequence` position it was taken at, the full
363	`state` summary, and `created_at`.
364	
365	### Webhook notifications
366	
367	Subscriptions declared on a workflow or an execution deliver outbound webhook
368	messages when business events occur. Each subscription contains exactly:
369	
370	- `url`: a non-empty `http` or `https` address to POST to;
371	- `events`: a non-empty array of event types without duplicates, drawn from
372	  `node_completed`, `execution_completed`, `execution_terminated`, and
373	  `approval_decided` (a termination is the same event type whatever its
374	  reason);
375	- `timeout_seconds` (optional): a positive number of seconds to wait for each
376	  delivery attempt, defaulting to 5;
377	- `max_attempts` (optional): an integer between 1 and 10, defaulting to 1.
378	
379	Any other field, a missing `url` or `events`, a mistyped value, an empty or
380	duplicated event list, an unknown event type, an empty or non-http(s) `url`,
381	a non-finite number, a non-positive timeout or attempt count, or more than
382	ten attempts is a 400 `validation_error` and rejects the whole request — no
383	workflow, execution, or subscription is partially written.
384	
385	When a subscribed event occurs, a JSON message is POSTed to each matching
386	target immediately: the body carries `event_type`, `execution_id`, and the
387	event's details (such as `node_id` for a completed node or `approver` for an
388	approval decision). Each delivery request carries an `Idempotency-Key`
389	header; retries of the same event reuse the same key, and different events
390	never share a key. A delivery is attempted at most the subscription's
391	`max_attempts` times, with an increasing backoff between attempts. An
392	unreachable target, a timeout, or a non-2xx response marks the attempt as
393	failed, but a failed delivery never changes the outcome of the call that
394	triggered it.
395	
396	Deliveries do not append execution events, do not add fields to the execution
397	state, and are never triggered by replay, recovery, or queries, so
398	checkpoints and replay conclusions are unaffected. An execution that declares
399	no subscriptions keeps exactly the same state, event stream, and advancement
400	results as before.
401	
402	### Inspect the delivery history
403	
404	```http
405	GET /executions/run-1/deliveries
406	```
407	
408	Returns `{"deliveries": [...]}` in the order the events occurred. Each record
409	gives its `sequence`, the subscription `url`, the `event_type`, the
410	`event_sequence` that triggered it, the delivery `idempotency_key`, the final
411	`status` (`delivered` or `failed`), the `attempt_count`, an `attempts` list
412	recording each try's `status_code` or `error` (so a retry that eventually
413	succeeds is visible attempt by attempt), and `occurred_at`. Querying the
414	history of a missing execution returns 404 `not_found` and records nothing.
415	Every delivery attempt is recorded, including one whose history record itself
416	could not be written: such a failure is not swallowed — it is retried once in
417	a fresh write carrying `status` `failed` and a `persistence_error` describing
418	the write failure, so the attempt remains visible whenever the database can
419	accept it (and is logged rather than silently dropped if it cannot).
420	
421	### Schedules
422	
423	A workflow may declare a schedule so the service creates executions
424	automatically. The declaration happens at workflow creation (a `schedule`
425	field next to `id` and `nodes`) or later through the update endpoint, and it
426	takes effect from the moment it is stored. A schedule contains exactly:
427	
428	- `interval_seconds`: a positive integer number of seconds between runs —
429	  or, alternatively, `cron`: a five-field cron expression (`minute hour
430	  day-of-month month day-of-week`) whose fields support `*`, `*/step`,
431	  single values, ranges `a-b`, ranges with steps `a-b/step`, and
432	  comma-separated lists, with 0 and 7 both meaning Sunday. Exactly one of
433	  `interval_seconds` and `cron` must be present;
434	- `input`: the object used as the execution input of every created run;
435	- `missed_policy`: either `catch_up` or `skip`.
436	
437	Whenever a period of the plan comes due, the service creates one execution
438	for the workflow with the declared input. The created execution is exactly a
439	manually created one: it starts `running` with the same state shape and the
440	usual `execution_started` event, and advancing, approvals, leases, retries,
441	timeouts, and cancellation all behave identically. The trigger itself writes
442	nothing into the created execution's event stream and adds no fields to its
443	state; the schedule's own record of when it fired and which execution it
444	created is exposed through the status query below.
445	
446	Creation is idempotent per schedule period: a repeated trigger or a repeated
447	request for the same period returns the same execution and never creates a
448	second one, under either missed policy. When periods were missed — the
449	schedule was paused, or the service was not running — `catch_up` makes up
450	exactly the single most recent missed period, while `skip` makes up none;
451	neither policy ever creates more than one execution for the same period.
452	
453	An invalid declaration rejects the whole request with 400
454	`validation_error` and writes nothing: a non-positive or non-integer
455	`interval_seconds`, a cron expression with other than five fields, out-of
456	range values, or unparseable fragments, declaring both `interval_seconds`
457	and `cron`, a `missed_policy` other than `catch_up` or `skip`, a missing or
458	mistyped `input`, or any unknown field.
459	
460	### Declare or replace a schedule
461	
462	```http
463	PUT /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule
464	Idempotency-Key: schedule-request-1
465	
466	{"interval_seconds":3600,"input":{"mode":"nightly"},"missed_policy":"catch_up"}
467	```
468	
469	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body is validated exactly
470	like a schedule declared at creation time, and the response is the schedule
471	status. Updating replaces the plan and re-anchors it at the update time; the
472	paused flag is kept. A missing workflow returns 404 `not_found`, an invalid
473	plan 400 `validation_error` with no partial write, and reusing an
474	idempotency key from another operation is a 409 `conflict`.
475	
476	### Inspect the schedule status
477	
478	```http
479	GET /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule
480	```
481	
482	Returns the declared plan as given (`interval_seconds` or `cron`, the
483	`input`, and the `missed_policy`), whether the schedule is currently
484	`paused`, the `last_triggered_at` time, and the `last_execution_id` of the
485	most recently created execution (both `null` until the first trigger). A
486	workflow that never declared a schedule returns the definite empty result
487	`{"schedule":null}`, and a missing workflow returns 404 `not_found`.
488	
489	### Pause and resume a schedule
490	
491	```http
492	POST /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule/pause
493	Idempotency-Key: pause-request-1
494	
495	{}
496	```
497	
498	```http
499	POST /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule/resume
500	Idempotency-Key: resume-request-1
501	
502	{}
503	```
504	
505	Both bodies must be empty objects; a missing or mistyped body, an unknown
506	field, or a non-finite number is a 400 `validation_error`. While paused, due
507	periods create no executions. Resuming settles the periods that came due
508	during the pause according to the missed policy: `catch_up` immediately
509	creates the single most recent missed run, `skip` creates none. Pausing or
510	resuming a workflow that has no schedule, or any schedule operation on a
511	missing workflow, returns 404 `not_found`; reusing an idempotency key across
512	operations returns 409 `conflict`. Both responses carry the schedule status.
513	
514	Workflows that declare no schedule are unaffected: their creation,
515	advancement, approvals, deliveries, checkpoints, recovery, and replay behave
516	exactly as before, with no additional fields or events.
517	
518	### Checkpoints
519	
520	Every successful `advance` that settles a node boundary — a task is
521	completed, or a failure is submitted (whether it retries or exhausts the
522	attempts) — writes a checkpoint in the same transaction as the state update
523	and event append. The checkpoint stores the complete state summary at that
524	boundary, including completed, skipped, and failed nodes, condition results,
525	outputs, attempts with their unfinished retry counts, and the status and
526	current iteration of every loop (with the per-iteration records), together
527	with the position of the last written event. Because the checkpoint matches
528	the stored state at that position, recovery can continue without replaying or
529	duplicating any node output.
530	
531	Checkpoints do not add fields to the execution state and do not append events:
532	an execution that declares no retries, timeout, or loops keeps exactly the
533	same state shape and event stream as before.
534	
535	### Complete the next ready node
536	
537	```http
538	POST /executions/run-1/advance
539	Idempotency-Key: advance-request-1
540	
541	{"output":{"reservation_id":"r-9"}}
542	```
543	
544	The lexicographically first ready task is completed. The response contains the
545	updated execution. Before that, each call first evaluates all ready conditions
546	in deterministic order and skips tasks whose `run_if` does not match; if this
547	automatic processing finishes the execution, the current state is returned and
548	the submitted output is not consumed. When every node is completed or skipped,
549	the status becomes `completed`.
550	
551	Instead of an output, a failure can be submitted for the same ready task:
552	
553	```http
554	POST /executions/run-1/advance
555	Idempotency-Key: advance-request-2
556	
557	{"failure":{"reason":"gateway timeout"}}
558	```
559	
560	The body must contain exactly one of `output` or `failure`, and `failure`
561	carries exactly a `reason` string. Either body may additionally carry a
562	`worker_id` string identifying the lease holder when the execution's work
563	item has been claimed (see "Claim a work item"). A failed task appends a `node_failed`
564	event recording the attempt number and reason. While the task has retries
565	left it returns to the ready set and a `node_retried` event records the next
566	attempt number; otherwise the task is permanently failed and the execution
567	terminates with reason `retries_exhausted`. The same rules apply to tasks
568	inside loop bodies, which are retried within their current iteration.
569	
570	Execution state includes `completed_nodes` (which also lists evaluated
571	conditions), `skipped_nodes`, `failed_nodes`, `condition_results`, `outputs`,
572	and `attempts`. `attempts` maps each attempted task to its current `attempt`
573	number and its `failures` count; loop body tasks track the same per iteration.
574	Executions of workflows that declare approval points additionally expose
575	`waiting_approval` (`null`, or the pending point's `node_id`, `approvers`, and
576	loop context) and the `approvals` record list. Each condition evaluation
577	appends a `condition_evaluated` event and each skip a `node_skipped` event to
578	the execution stream.
579	
580	### Cancel an execution
581	
582	```http
583	POST /executions/run-1/cancel
584	Idempotency-Key: cancel-request-1
585	```
586	
587	A running execution is terminated immediately with termination reason
588	`cancelled`. Cancelling a completed or already terminated execution returns
589	its state unchanged, and cancelling a missing execution returns 404.
590	
591	Execution status is `running`, `completed`, or `terminated`. A terminated
592	execution records exactly one `termination_reason` — `retries_exhausted`,
593	`rejected`, `timeout`, or `cancelled` — and appends a single
594	`execution_terminated` event; completed executions keep a `null` termination
595	reason and their own `execution_completed` event. Advancing a terminated
596	execution returns its state unchanged without consuming the submitted output
597	or failure; a decision against one only succeeds as a repeat of the decision
598	that rejected it, and otherwise conflicts.
599	
600	### Claim a work item
601	
602	```http
603	POST /executions/run-1/claim
604	Idempotency-Key: claim-request-1
605	
606	{"worker_id":"worker-7","lease_seconds":30}
607	```
608	
609	Claiming is how an external worker takes ownership of a running execution
610	before advancing its ready tasks. `worker_id` is a non-empty string and
611	`lease_seconds` is an optional positive number of seconds (default 30). The
612	response contains the claimed `work_item` (its `execution_id` and
613	`workflow_id`) and a `lease` recording the `worker_id`, the `lease_seconds`
614	duration, the `expires_at` deadline, and the `heartbeat_at` active time.
615	Each work item is held by at most one worker at a time: claiming a work
616	item whose lease is still active — even by the same worker — is a 409
617	`conflict`. Claiming a completed or terminated execution returns the
618	definite empty result `{"work_item":null,"lease":null}` and absorbs no
619	input, and claiming a missing execution returns 404.
620	
621	While a work item is held, results are submitted through the usual
622	`advance` entry by including the holder's identity:
623	
624	```http
625	POST /executions/run-1/advance
626	Idempotency-Key: advance-request-3
627	
628	{"output":{"reservation_id":"r-9"},"worker_id":"worker-7"}
629	```
630	
631	Submitting results for a work item held by another worker, or after the
632	lease has expired, is a 409 `conflict` that does not change execution
633	state. An execution that never claimed a work item accepts `advance`
634	exactly as before, and its state fields and event stream are identical to
635	an execution without any claim.
636	
637	When a lease expires, the work item returns to the claimable set and may be
638	claimed again by the same or another worker. The second claim continues
639	from the materialized state: node outputs and results recorded by the
640	earlier holder are never advanced or recorded twice, and every written
641	output belongs to the single advance that submitted it.
642	
643	### Renew a lease
644	
645	```http
646	POST /executions/run-1/heartbeat
647	Idempotency-Key: heartbeat-request-1
648	
649	{"worker_id":"worker-7"}
650	```
651	
652	Within the lease period the holder may heartbeat to extend `expires_at` by
653	the lease duration and refresh the `heartbeat_at` active time; the response
654	carries the updated `lease`. A heartbeat never advances nodes, writes
655	outputs, or appends node events. A heartbeat from another worker or after
656	the lease expired is a 409 `conflict`; a heartbeat for a missing execution
657	or an execution with no claimed work item is a 404 `not_found`.
658	
659	### Release a work item
660	
661	```http
662	POST /executions/run-1/release
663	Idempotency-Key: release-request-1
664	
665	{"worker_id":"worker-7"}
666	```
667	
668	Releasing invalidates the lease immediately and returns the work item to
669	the claimable set, so it can be claimed again right away; progress already
670	made and the recorded events are unchanged. Releasing with another
671	worker's identity or after expiry is a 409 `conflict`; releasing for a
672	missing execution or an execution with no claimed work item is a 404
673	`not_found`.
674	
675	Claims, heartbeats, and releases append no events and add no fields to the
676	execution state, so replay, checkpoints, and recovery are unaffected.
677	Leases live in the same SQLite database as the execution state, so
678	unexpired leases and claim ownership remain valid after the service
679	restarts.
680	
681	### Recover from a checkpoint
682	
683	```http
684	POST /executions/run-1/recover
685	Idempotency-Key: recover-request-1
686	
687	{"from":"latest_checkpoint"}
688	```
689	
690	Recovery rebuilds a running execution from its latest checkpoint and returns
691	the rebuilt execution. It appends no events and changes no state: the rebuilt
692	execution is exactly the materialized state, and a subsequent replay has the
693	same conclusion as before the interruption. After recovery, further
694	`advance` calls continue from the checkpoint, so node outputs, failure
695	reasons, attempt numbers, and loop iteration ownership are identical to an
696	uninterrupted run; failure records for tasks inside a loop body still carry
697	their loop id and current iteration. Recovery works after the service has
698	been restarted, because checkpoints live in the same SQLite database as the
699	execution state and events.
700	
701	A completed execution is returned unchanged, producing no new events. A
702	terminated execution is likewise returned unchanged and the operation
703	absorbs no input; if a timeout or cancellation takes effect between
704	checkpoint writes, termination takes precedence over recovery. Events and
705	checkpoints remain queryable after cancellation or timeout, and their replay
706	stays consistent with the materialized state.
707	
708	Recovering a missing execution returns 404. Recovering an execution that has
709	no checkpoint, or whose latest checkpoint cannot be parsed, returns 409
710	`conflict`. A missing `from` field, a wrong type, or an unknown recovery
711	origin is a 400 `validation_error`; a non-finite number in the body is
712	rejected the same way as every other request. Reusing an idempotency key
713	already used by another operation (including an `advance` or `cancel` on the
714	same execution) returns 409 `conflict`.
715	
716	### Replay
717	
718	```http
719	POST /executions/run-1/replay
720	```
721	
722	Rebuilds state solely from the execution event stream and compares it with the
723	stored materialized state. A successful response contains `consistent: true`
724	and the rebuilt execution.
725	
726	## Errors
727	
728	Errors use this shape:
729	
730	```json
731	{"error":{"code":"validation_error","message":"human readable detail"}}
732	```
733	
734	Validation errors return 400, missing resources return 404, and conflicts
735	return 409. An empty `X-Tenant-Id` header value is a validation error; quota
736	declarations require a tenant and positive integer limits, validated by the
737	same rules as every other body (no non-finite numbers, no unknown fields).
738	Reusing a workflow or execution identifier, or reusing an idempotency key
739	across different operations (within the same tenant), is a conflict.
740	Exceeding a tenant's declared workflow or execution quota is also a `409
741	conflict`, with the word "quota" in the message so it can be distinguished
742	from an identifier conflict; the rejected request writes nothing. Referencing
743	a resource owned by another tenant is a missing resource (`404
744	not_found`), indistinguishable from one that does not exist, so existence is
745	never revealed across tenants. A `retries` value that is negative, non-integer, or greater than
746	10, and a non-positive `timeout_seconds`, are validation errors. A malformed
747	subscription — a missing or mistyped field, an unknown field, an empty or
748	duplicated event list, an unknown event type, an empty or non-http(s) `url`,
749	a non-positive timeout or attempt count, or more than ten attempts — is a
750	validation error that rejects the whole request without partial writes, and
751	querying the delivery history of a missing execution is a missing resource. An approval
752	point with an empty approver list, a duplicate or non-string approver, an
753	approval on a non-task node, and a decision body that is malformed or carries
754	a decision other than `approved` or `rejected` are validation errors.
755	A decision by an approver who is
756	not listed for the pending point, or any decision against an execution that
757	has no pending approval point (other than a repeat of the decision that
758	resolved the latest one), is a conflict. Claiming a work item whose lease is
759	still active, submitting results for a work item held by another worker or
760	after the lease expired, and heartbeating or releasing a lease held by
761	another worker are conflicts, while heartbeating or releasing an execution
762	with no claimed work item is a missing resource. Recovering a missing
763	execution is a missing resource, while recovering an execution that has no
764	checkpoint or whose latest checkpoint is unparseable is a conflict; an
765	invalid recover body is a validation error. An invalid schedule declaration —
766	a non-positive or non-integer interval, a malformed or out-of-range cron
767	expression, declaring both an interval and a cron plan, an unknown missed
768	policy, or an unknown field — is a validation error that rejects the whole
769	request without partial writes; pausing, resuming, or updating the schedule
770	of a missing workflow, or pausing and resuming a workflow that has no
771	schedule, is a missing resource, and a malformed pause or resume body is a
772	validation error. Request bodies must not contain
773	non-finite numbers (`NaN`, `Infinity`, or overflowing values such as `1e400`);
774	they are rejected with 400. Finite floats keep their full precision, including negative zero
775	(`-0.0`), and every response body ends with a single newline.
776	
777	## Tests
778	
779	```bash
780	PYTHONPATH=src python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
781	```
782

# ChronicleFlow

ChronicleFlow is a small backend for durable workflow orchestration. It stores
workflow definitions, execution state, and an append-only event history in
SQLite so an execution can be inspected and replayed deterministically.

The initial release intentionally supports a compact public contract:

- workflows are directed acyclic graphs of `task`, `condition`, and bounded
  `loop` nodes;
- executions advance one ready task at a time, evaluating conditions and
  skipping unmatched branches automatically;
- task nodes may declare a bounded number of retries: a submitted failure
  re-queues the node until the retries are exhausted, which terminates the
  execution;
- a task node may declare an approval point with the people allowed to decide
  it; advancing parks the task in a waiting state until an approver approves
  (completing it with the submitted output) or rejects (terminating the
  execution with reason `rejected`);
- executions may declare a timeout in seconds, after which they terminate and
  no longer accept output, and they may be cancelled explicitly;
- loop nodes repeat their body a bounded number of times, re-evaluating a
  continue condition at the loop boundaries;
- every state transition is appended to the execution event stream;
- replay rebuilds execution state from the recorded events;
- a checkpoint is written at every node boundary, capturing the state
  summary and event position, so an execution can be recovered from the
  latest checkpoint after a restart;
- workers may claim a running execution to receive a work item with a
  time-bounded lease, renew the lease with heartbeats, and release it;
  while a lease is active only its holder may submit results, and an
  expired or released lease returns the work item to the claimable set;
- duplicate commands with the same idempotency key return the original result;
- workflows and executions may declare webhook subscriptions, and matching
  business events are delivered to the declared targets with bounded retries,
  each delivery recorded in a per-execution history;
- a workflow may declare a schedule — a fixed interval in seconds or a
  five-field cron plan — and the service automatically creates one execution
  per due period with the declared input; schedules can be paused and
  resumed, and periods missed while paused are either caught up once or
  skipped, according to the declared missed policy.

## Requirements

- Python 3.11 or newer
- no third-party runtime dependencies

## Run the service

```bash
PYTHONPATH=src python -m chronicleflow.server --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --database chronicleflow.db
```

The process prints `ChronicleFlow listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080` after it
has bound the port.

## HTTP API

All request and response bodies are JSON. Unknown fields are rejected.

### Tenants and quotas

A request may declare a tenant by sending the `X-Tenant-Id` header with a
non-empty identifier. Every workflow, execution, schedule, schedule status,
and delivery history record is scoped to the tenant of the request that
created it: queries and operations only ever see data belonging to that
tenant, and different tenants may use the same workflow or execution
identifiers without colliding. Referencing another tenant's resource — for
example advancing, deciding, claiming, cancelling, recovering, replaying, or
reading the events, checkpoints, deliveries, or schedule of an execution or
workflow owned by another tenant — is answered exactly like a reference to a
missing resource: `404 not_found`, with no indication that the resource
exists elsewhere. An execution created in one tenant can only reference a
workflow of the same tenant; referencing an unseen workflow identifier is the
usual `404 not_found`.

The header applies to every workflow, execution, and schedule entry point,
including creation, advancement, approval decisions, lease operations,
cancellation, recovery, replay, and all history and status queries. An empty
`X-Tenant-Id` value is a `400 validation_error`. Requests that omit the
header entirely keep using the single legacy namespace, whose advancement,
approvals, leases, retries, timeouts, cancellation, checkpoints, recovery,
scheduling, and replay behavior is byte-for-byte unchanged: the tenant is
stored only as database scope, never added to a state field or event payload,
and state shapes and event streams gain no new fields. Idempotency keys are
scoped per tenant as well, so tenants can never see or collide with each
other's keys; reusing a key for another operation within the same tenant is
the usual `409 conflict`.

A tenant may declare quotas bounding how many workflows and executions it may
hold:

```http
PUT /quotas
Idempotency-Key: quota-request-1
X-Tenant-Id: acme

{"workflows": 10, "executions": 100}
```

`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body must contain exactly
`workflows` and `executions`, each a positive integer; a non-positive,
non-integer, boolean, or non-finite value, a missing or extra field, or a
non-object body is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing. Both quota
routes require a tenant: calling them without `X-Tenant-Id` (or with an empty
one) is a `400 validation_error`. The response is
`{"quota":{"workflows":10,"executions":100}}`; declaring again replaces the
limits (re-anchoring nothing else). Lowering a limit below the current
holding deletes no existing data — existing workflows and executions stay
fully usable — it only rejects later writes that would exceed the new limit.

```http
GET /quotas
X-Tenant-Id: acme
```

Returns the declared quota, or the definite empty result `{"quota":null}`
when the tenant has declared none.

When a write would take the tenant past either limit, the whole request is
rejected with `409 conflict` and an error message that names the quota (for
example `quota exceeded: tenant already holds 10 workflows (quota limit is
10)`), so callers can tell quota rejection apart from an ordinary identifier
conflict. The rejection performs no partial write: nothing is inserted and
previously stored data is unaffected, exactly as for validation failures.

A schedule firing on time creates its execution in the schedule's tenant and
that execution counts against the tenant's execution quota. When the tenant
is at its execution limit, the due period creates no execution and the
schedule is left unchanged — its cursor, `last_triggered_at`, and
`last_execution_id` stay as they were — so the period is settled on a later
pass once capacity exists, under the usual per-period idempotence. Delivery
history follows the tenant of the execution it belongs to.

### Health

```http
GET /health
```

Returns `{"status":"ok"}`.

### Create a workflow

```http
POST /workflows
Idempotency-Key: workflow-request-1

{
  "id": "order-flow",
  "nodes": [
    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
    {"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
  ]
}
```

Returns HTTP 201 with the stored workflow. Node identifiers must be unique,
dependencies must exist, and cycles are rejected.

A workflow may also declare webhook `subscriptions` alongside its nodes:

```json
{
  "id": "order-flow",
  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/orders", "events": ["execution_completed"]}]
}
```

See "Webhook notifications" below for the subscription shape and delivery
semantics; the subscriptions apply to every execution of the workflow.

A workflow may also declare a `schedule` alongside its nodes:

```json
{
  "id": "nightly-orders",
  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
  "schedule": {"interval_seconds": 3600, "input": {"mode": "nightly"}, "missed_policy": "catch_up"}
}
```

See "Schedules" below for the declaration shape and the trigger semantics.

Besides `task`, a node may have `kind` set to `condition`:

```json
{"id": "is_vip", "kind": "condition", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "path": "customer.vip", "equals": true}
```

`path` is a non-empty dot-separated path into the execution input and `equals`
is a JSON scalar (string, number, boolean, or null). A condition is evaluated
automatically once its dependencies complete: the input value at `path` is
compared with `equals` by JSON type and value, and a missing path evaluates to
`false`.

A task may carry an optional `run_if` guard:

```json
{"id": "expedite", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["is_vip"], "run_if": {"condition_id": "is_vip", "expected": true}}
```

`condition_id` must reference a `condition` node that is also listed in the
task's `depends_on`. When the condition's result differs from `expected`, the
task is marked as skipped: it receives no output and still satisfies the
dependencies of its successors.

A task may declare how many times it is retried after a failure:

```json
{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "retries": 3}
```

`retries` is an integer between 0 and 10 and defaults to 0, meaning the task
is attempted only once. Each failure submitted through `advance` consumes one
attempt; while retries remain, the task returns to the ready set and is
advanced again. When a failure arrives with no retries left, the task is
permanently failed and the whole execution terminates with termination reason
`retries_exhausted`.

A task may instead declare an approval point:

```json
{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "approval": {"approvers": ["alice", "bob"]}}
```

`approval` contains exactly `approvers`, a non-empty array of approver
identifier strings without duplicates; an empty list, a duplicate entry, or a
non-string entry is a validation error, and only `task` nodes may carry an
approval point. When an `advance` reaches a ready task with an approval point,
the task does not complete and the submitted output or failure is not
consumed: an `approval_requested` event is appended (recording the node, its
approvers, and, inside a loop body, the loop id and iteration) and the
execution stays `running`, parked in a waiting state returned under
`waiting_approval`. Further `advance` calls return the current state without
writing output, completing the node, or appending events; only a decision can
move the task.

### Submit an approval decision

```http
POST /executions/run-1/decision
Idempotency-Key: decision-request-1

{"approver":"alice","decision":"approved","output":{"charge_id":"c-3"}}
```

`decision` is either `approved` or `rejected`. An approved decision carries
exactly `approver`, `decision`, and an `output` object; the task completes with
that output and its successors become available in the usual way. A rejected
decision carries exactly `approver`, `decision`, and a `reason` string; the
task is permanently failed (it is listed under `failed_nodes`) and the
execution terminates with termination reason `rejected`. Either decision
appends an `approval_decided` event with the node, approver, decision, and (on
rejection) the reason, and the approval record is kept under `approvals`. A
request whose approver is not in the point's approver list is a 409
`conflict`, and a malformed body or a decision value other than `approved` or
`rejected` is a 400 `validation_error`; neither changes execution state.
Repeating the decision that already resolved the most recent approval point —
the same approver and decision with the same output or rejection reason —
returns the first result and neither advances the node again nor appends
another event; any other decision against an execution with no pending
approval point is a 409 `conflict`, and deciding a missing execution returns
404.

While an execution is parked at an approval point it remains `running`, so a
cancellation takes effect immediately with the usual `cancelled` termination
reason, and a reached timeout terminates it with `timeout`; both dismiss the
pending point and the execution then no longer accepts decisions or output.
The waiting point, its request and decision events, and the termination
reason are rebuilt solely from the event stream on replay, and the parked and
decided node boundaries are checkpointed like every other boundary, so
waiting points and recorded decisions remain valid after a restart. Approval
state is added to an execution only when its workflow declares at least one
approval point; workflows without approvals keep exactly the previous state
shape and event stream.

A node may also have `kind` set to `loop`, describing a bounded repeated
segment:

```json
{"id": "retry", "kind": "loop", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "entry": "attempt", "condition": "keep_trying", "max_iterations": 3}
```

A loop node contains exactly `id`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `entry`, `condition`,
and `max_iterations`; any other field is rejected as unknown. `entry` names a
`task` node, `condition` names a `condition` node, and `max_iterations` is an
integer between 1 and 100. The loop body is the entry task plus every node
reachable from it through `depends_on`; the body keeps the usual DAG rules and
must contain the referenced condition. The loop's own dependencies must be
completed or skipped before the first iteration may start, they must not
overlap the body, bodies of different loops must not overlap or nest, and
nodes outside a body must not depend on nodes inside it (they depend on the
loop node instead).

When the loop's dependencies are satisfied, the loop evaluates its condition
against the execution input (same JSON type and value comparison as condition
nodes; a missing path is `false`). If it is `false`, the loop completes with
zero iterations and end reason `condition_false`. If it is `true`, the first
iteration starts and the body advances one ready task per `advance` call in
the usual deterministic order; conditions and `run_if` skips inside the body
are re-evaluated every iteration, and task outputs belong only to the current
iteration. Once every body node is completed or skipped, the condition is
evaluated again: `true` starts the next iteration, `false` ends the loop with
`condition_false`, and reaching `max_iterations` ends it with
`iteration_limit` after that iteration finishes. Ending the loop completes
the loop node and releases the dependencies of its successors.

Execution state exposes each loop under `loops`: `status`, the
`current_iteration`, one entry per iteration with its own `completed_nodes`,
`skipped_nodes`, `condition_results`, and `outputs`, and the single
`end_reason` (`condition_false` or `iteration_limit`). The event stream
records `iteration_started`, `loop_condition_evaluated`, and `loop_completed`
events alongside the usual per-node ones, so replay rebuilds loop state
exactly.

### Start an execution

```http
POST /executions
Idempotency-Key: execution-request-1

{"id":"run-1","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{"order_id":"o-7"}}
```

Returns HTTP 201. The execution starts in `running` state.

An execution may declare a timeout:

```json
{"id":"run-2","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{},"timeout_seconds":30}
```

`timeout_seconds` is a positive number of seconds counted from the moment the
execution starts. Once the deadline passes, the execution terminates with
termination reason `timeout` and no longer accepts output. Executions without
a timeout never expire.

An execution may also declare its own webhook `subscriptions`, which apply in
addition to the ones its workflow declares:

```json
{
  "id": "run-3",
  "workflow_id": "order-flow",
  "input": {},
  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/ops", "events": ["node_completed"], "max_attempts": 3}]
}
```

### Inspect an execution

```http
GET /executions/run-1
GET /executions/run-1/events
GET /executions/run-1/checkpoints
```

The first endpoint returns the materialized state. The second returns the
ordered event stream. The third returns the ordered checkpoints; each entry
gives its `sequence`, the `event_sequence` position it was taken at, the full
`state` summary, and `created_at`.

### Webhook notifications

Subscriptions declared on a workflow or an execution deliver outbound webhook
messages when business events occur. Each subscription contains exactly:

- `url`: a non-empty `http` or `https` address to POST to;
- `events`: a non-empty array of event types without duplicates, drawn from
  `node_completed`, `execution_completed`, `execution_terminated`, and
  `approval_decided` (a termination is the same event type whatever its
  reason);
- `timeout_seconds` (optional): a positive number of seconds to wait for each
  delivery attempt, defaulting to 5;
- `max_attempts` (optional): an integer between 1 and 10, defaulting to 1.

Any other field, a missing `url` or `events`, a mistyped value, an empty or
duplicated event list, an unknown event type, an empty or non-http(s) `url`,
a non-finite number, a non-positive timeout or attempt count, or more than
ten attempts is a 400 `validation_error` and rejects the whole request — no
workflow, execution, or subscription is partially written.

When a subscribed event occurs, a JSON message is POSTed to each matching
target immediately: the body carries `event_type`, `execution_id`, and the
event's details (such as `node_id` for a completed node or `approver` for an
approval decision). Each delivery request carries an `Idempotency-Key`
header; retries of the same event reuse the same key, and different events
never share a key. A delivery is attempted at most the subscription's
`max_attempts` times, with an increasing backoff between attempts. An
unreachable target, a timeout, or a non-2xx response marks the attempt as
failed, but a failed delivery never changes the outcome of the call that
triggered it.

Deliveries do not append execution events, do not add fields to the execution
state, and are never triggered by replay, recovery, or queries, so
checkpoints and replay conclusions are unaffected. An execution that declares
no subscriptions keeps exactly the same state, event stream, and advancement
results as before.

### Inspect the delivery history

```http
GET /executions/run-1/deliveries
```

Returns `{"deliveries": [...]}` in the order the events occurred. Each record
gives its `sequence`, the subscription `url`, the `event_type`, the
`event_sequence` that triggered it, the delivery `idempotency_key`, the final
`status` (`delivered` or `failed`), the `attempt_count`, an `attempts` list
recording each try's `status_code` or `error` (so a retry that eventually
succeeds is visible attempt by attempt), and `occurred_at`. Querying the
history of a missing execution returns 404 `not_found` and records nothing.
Every delivery attempt is recorded, including one whose history record itself
could not be written: such a failure is not swallowed — it is retried once in
a fresh write carrying `status` `failed` and a `persistence_error` describing
the write failure, so the attempt remains visible whenever the database can
accept it (and is logged rather than silently dropped if it cannot).

### Schedules

A workflow may declare a schedule so the service creates executions
automatically. The declaration happens at workflow creation (a `schedule`
field next to `id` and `nodes`) or later through the update endpoint, and it
takes effect from the moment it is stored. A schedule contains exactly:

- `interval_seconds`: a positive integer number of seconds between runs —
  or, alternatively, `cron`: a five-field cron expression (`minute hour
  day-of-month month day-of-week`) whose fields support `*`, `*/step`,
  single values, ranges `a-b`, ranges with steps `a-b/step`, and
  comma-separated lists, with 0 and 7 both meaning Sunday. Exactly one of
  `interval_seconds` and `cron` must be present;
- `input`: the object used as the execution input of every created run;
- `missed_policy`: either `catch_up` or `skip`.

Whenever a period of the plan comes due, the service creates one execution
for the workflow with the declared input. The created execution is exactly a
manually created one: it starts `running` with the same state shape and the
usual `execution_started` event, and advancing, approvals, leases, retries,
timeouts, and cancellation all behave identically. The trigger itself writes
nothing into the created execution's event stream and adds no fields to its
state; the schedule's own record of when it fired and which execution it
created is exposed through the status query below.

Creation is idempotent per schedule period: a repeated trigger or a repeated
request for the same period returns the same execution and never creates a
second one, under either missed policy. When periods were missed — the
schedule was paused, or the service was not running — `catch_up` makes up
exactly the single most recent missed period, while `skip` makes up none;
neither policy ever creates more than one execution for the same period.

An invalid declaration rejects the whole request with 400
`validation_error` and writes nothing: a non-positive or non-integer
`interval_seconds`, a cron expression with other than five fields, out-of
range values, or unparseable fragments, declaring both `interval_seconds`
and `cron`, a `missed_policy` other than `catch_up` or `skip`, a missing or
mistyped `input`, or any unknown field.

### Declare or replace a schedule

```http
PUT /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule
Idempotency-Key: schedule-request-1

{"interval_seconds":3600,"input":{"mode":"nightly"},"missed_policy":"catch_up"}
```

`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body is validated exactly
like a schedule declared at creation time, and the response is the schedule
status. Updating replaces the plan and re-anchors it at the update time; the
paused flag is kept. A missing workflow returns 404 `not_found`, an invalid
plan 400 `validation_error` with no partial write, and reusing an
idempotency key from another operation is a 409 `conflict`.

### Inspect the schedule status

```http
GET /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule
```

Returns the declared plan as given (`interval_seconds` or `cron`, the
`input`, and the `missed_policy`), whether the schedule is currently
`paused`, the `last_triggered_at` time, and the `last_execution_id` of the
most recently created execution (both `null` until the first trigger). A
workflow that never declared a schedule returns the definite empty result
`{"schedule":null}`, and a missing workflow returns 404 `not_found`.

### Pause and resume a schedule

```http
POST /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule/pause
Idempotency-Key: pause-request-1

{}
```

```http
POST /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule/resume
Idempotency-Key: resume-request-1

{}
```

Both bodies must be empty objects; a missing or mistyped body, an unknown
field, or a non-finite number is a 400 `validation_error`. While paused, due
periods create no executions. Resuming settles the periods that came due
during the pause according to the missed policy: `catch_up` immediately
creates the single most recent missed run, `skip` creates none. Pausing or
resuming a workflow that has no schedule, or any schedule operation on a
missing workflow, returns 404 `not_found`; reusing an idempotency key across
operations returns 409 `conflict`. Both responses carry the schedule status.

Workflows that declare no schedule are unaffected: their creation,
advancement, approvals, deliveries, checkpoints, recovery, and replay behave
exactly as before, with no additional fields or events.

### Checkpoints

Every successful `advance` that settles a node boundary — a task is
completed, or a failure is submitted (whether it retries or exhausts the
attempts) — writes a checkpoint in the same transaction as the state update
and event append. The checkpoint stores the complete state summary at that
boundary, including completed, skipped, and failed nodes, condition results,
outputs, attempts with their unfinished retry counts, and the status and
current iteration of every loop (with the per-iteration records), together
with the position of the last written event. Because the checkpoint matches
the stored state at that position, recovery can continue without replaying or
duplicating any node output.

Checkpoints do not add fields to the execution state and do not append events:
an execution that declares no retries, timeout, or loops keeps exactly the
same state shape and event stream as before.

### Complete the next ready node

```http
POST /executions/run-1/advance
Idempotency-Key: advance-request-1

{"output":{"reservation_id":"r-9"}}
```

The lexicographically first ready task is completed. The response contains the
updated execution. Before that, each call first evaluates all ready conditions
in deterministic order and skips tasks whose `run_if` does not match; if this
automatic processing finishes the execution, the current state is returned and
the submitted output is not consumed. When every node is completed or skipped,
the status becomes `completed`.

Instead of an output, a failure can be submitted for the same ready task:

```http
POST /executions/run-1/advance
Idempotency-Key: advance-request-2

{"failure":{"reason":"gateway timeout"}}
```

The body must contain exactly one of `output` or `failure`, and `failure`
carries exactly a `reason` string. Either body may additionally carry a
`worker_id` string identifying the lease holder when the execution's work
item has been claimed (see "Claim a work item"). A failed task appends a `node_failed`
event recording the attempt number and reason. While the task has retries
left it returns to the ready set and a `node_retried` event records the next
attempt number; otherwise the task is permanently failed and the execution
terminates with reason `retries_exhausted`. The same rules apply to tasks
inside loop bodies, which are retried within their current iteration.

Execution state includes `completed_nodes` (which also lists evaluated
conditions), `skipped_nodes`, `failed_nodes`, `condition_results`, `outputs`,
and `attempts`. `attempts` maps each attempted task to its current `attempt`
number and its `failures` count; loop body tasks track the same per iteration.
Executions of workflows that declare approval points additionally expose
`waiting_approval` (`null`, or the pending point's `node_id`, `approvers`, and
loop context) and the `approvals` record list. Each condition evaluation
appends a `condition_evaluated` event and each skip a `node_skipped` event to
the execution stream.

### Cancel an execution

```http
POST /executions/run-1/cancel
Idempotency-Key: cancel-request-1
```

A running execution is terminated immediately with termination reason
`cancelled`. Cancelling a completed or already terminated execution returns
its state unchanged, and cancelling a missing execution returns 404.

Execution status is `running`, `completed`, or `terminated`. A terminated
execution records exactly one `termination_reason` — `retries_exhausted`,
`rejected`, `timeout`, or `cancelled` — and appends a single
`execution_terminated` event; completed executions keep a `null` termination
reason and their own `execution_completed` event. Advancing a terminated
execution returns its state unchanged without consuming the submitted output
or failure; a decision against one only succeeds as a repeat of the decision
that rejected it, and otherwise conflicts.

### Claim a work item

```http
POST /executions/run-1/claim
Idempotency-Key: claim-request-1

{"worker_id":"worker-7","lease_seconds":30}
```

Claiming is how an external worker takes ownership of a running execution
before advancing its ready tasks. `worker_id` is a non-empty string and
`lease_seconds` is an optional positive number of seconds (default 30). The
response contains the claimed `work_item` (its `execution_id` and
`workflow_id`) and a `lease` recording the `worker_id`, the `lease_seconds`
duration, the `expires_at` deadline, and the `heartbeat_at` active time.
Each work item is held by at most one worker at a time: claiming a work
item whose lease is still active — even by the same worker — is a 409
`conflict`. Claiming a completed or terminated execution returns the
definite empty result `{"work_item":null,"lease":null}` and absorbs no
input, and claiming a missing execution returns 404.

While a work item is held, results are submitted through the usual
`advance` entry by including the holder's identity:

```http
POST /executions/run-1/advance
Idempotency-Key: advance-request-3

{"output":{"reservation_id":"r-9"},"worker_id":"worker-7"}
```

Submitting results for a work item held by another worker, or after the
lease has expired, is a 409 `conflict` that does not change execution
state. An execution that never claimed a work item accepts `advance`
exactly as before, and its state fields and event stream are identical to
an execution without any claim.

When a lease expires, the work item returns to the claimable set and may be
claimed again by the same or another worker. The second claim continues
from the materialized state: node outputs and results recorded by the
earlier holder are never advanced or recorded twice, and every written
output belongs to the single advance that submitted it.

### Renew a lease

```http
POST /executions/run-1/heartbeat
Idempotency-Key: heartbeat-request-1

{"worker_id":"worker-7"}
```

Within the lease period the holder may heartbeat to extend `expires_at` by
the lease duration and refresh the `heartbeat_at` active time; the response
carries the updated `lease`. A heartbeat never advances nodes, writes
outputs, or appends node events. A heartbeat from another worker or after
the lease expired is a 409 `conflict`; a heartbeat for a missing execution
or an execution with no claimed work item is a 404 `not_found`.

### Release a work item

```http
POST /executions/run-1/release
Idempotency-Key: release-request-1

{"worker_id":"worker-7"}
```

Releasing invalidates the lease immediately and returns the work item to
the claimable set, so it can be claimed again right away; progress already
made and the recorded events are unchanged. Releasing with another
worker's identity or after expiry is a 409 `conflict`; releasing for a
missing execution or an execution with no claimed work item is a 404
`not_found`.

Claims, heartbeats, and releases append no events and add no fields to the
execution state, so replay, checkpoints, and recovery are unaffected.
Leases live in the same SQLite database as the execution state, so
unexpired leases and claim ownership remain valid after the service
restarts.

### Recover from a checkpoint

```http
POST /executions/run-1/recover
Idempotency-Key: recover-request-1

{"from":"latest_checkpoint"}
```

Recovery rebuilds a running execution from its latest checkpoint and returns
the rebuilt execution. It appends no events and changes no state: the rebuilt
execution is exactly the materialized state, and a subsequent replay has the
same conclusion as before the interruption. After recovery, further
`advance` calls continue from the checkpoint, so node outputs, failure
reasons, attempt numbers, and loop iteration ownership are identical to an
uninterrupted run; failure records for tasks inside a loop body still carry
their loop id and current iteration. Recovery works after the service has
been restarted, because checkpoints live in the same SQLite database as the
execution state and events.

A completed execution is returned unchanged, producing no new events. A
terminated execution is likewise returned unchanged and the operation
absorbs no input; if a timeout or cancellation takes effect between
checkpoint writes, termination takes precedence over recovery. Events and
checkpoints remain queryable after cancellation or timeout, and their replay
stays consistent with the materialized state.

Recovering a missing execution returns 404. Recovering an execution that has
no checkpoint, or whose latest checkpoint cannot be parsed, returns 409
`conflict`. A missing `from` field, a wrong type, or an unknown recovery
origin is a 400 `validation_error`; a non-finite number in the body is
rejected the same way as every other request. Reusing an idempotency key
already used by another operation (including an `advance` or `cancel` on the
same execution) returns 409 `conflict`.

### Replay

```http
POST /executions/run-1/replay
```

Rebuilds state solely from the execution event stream and compares it with the
stored materialized state. A successful response contains `consistent: true`
and the rebuilt execution.

## Errors

Errors use this shape:

```json
{"error":{"code":"validation_error","message":"human readable detail"}}
```

Validation errors return 400, missing resources return 404, and conflicts
return 409. An empty `X-Tenant-Id` header value is a validation error; quota
declarations require a tenant and positive integer limits, validated by the
same rules as every other body (no non-finite numbers, no unknown fields).
Reusing a workflow or execution identifier, or reusing an idempotency key
across different operations (within the same tenant), is a conflict.
Exceeding a tenant's declared workflow or execution quota is also a `409
conflict`, with the word "quota" in the message so it can be distinguished
from an identifier conflict; the rejected request writes nothing. Referencing
a resource owned by another tenant is a missing resource (`404
not_found`), indistinguishable from one that does not exist, so existence is
never revealed across tenants. A `retries` value that is negative, non-integer, or greater than
10, and a non-positive `timeout_seconds`, are validation errors. A malformed
subscription — a missing or mistyped field, an unknown field, an empty or
duplicated event list, an unknown event type, an empty or non-http(s) `url`,
a non-positive timeout or attempt count, or more than ten attempts — is a
validation error that rejects the whole request without partial writes, and
querying the delivery history of a missing execution is a missing resource. An approval
point with an empty approver list, a duplicate or non-string approver, an
approval on a non-task node, and a decision body that is malformed or carries
a decision other than `approved` or `rejected` are validation errors.
A decision by an approver who is
not listed for the pending point, or any decision against an execution that
has no pending approval point (other than a repeat of the decision that
resolved the latest one), is a conflict. Claiming a work item whose lease is
still active, submitting results for a work item held by another worker or
after the lease expired, and heartbeating or releasing a lease held by
another worker are conflicts, while heartbeating or releasing an execution
with no claimed work item is a missing resource. Recovering a missing
execution is a missing resource, while recovering an execution that has no
checkpoint or whose latest checkpoint is unparseable is a conflict; an
invalid recover body is a validation error. An invalid schedule declaration —
a non-positive or non-integer interval, a malformed or out-of-range cron
expression, declaring both an interval and a cron plan, an unknown missed
policy, or an unknown field — is a validation error that rejects the whole
request without partial writes; pausing, resuming, or updating the schedule
of a missing workflow, or pausing and resuming a workflow that has no
schedule, is a missing resource, and a malformed pause or resume body is a
validation error. Request bodies must not contain
non-finite numbers (`NaN`, `Infinity`, or overflowing values such as `1e400`);
they are rejected with 400. Finite floats keep their full precision, including negative zero
(`-0.0`), and every response body ends with a single newline.

## Tests

```bash
PYTHONPATH=src python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
```

220	def _collect_loop_body(by_id: dict[str, Node], entry: str) -> set[str]:
221	    body: set[str] = set()

223	    while stack:
224	        node_id = stack.pop()

228	        stack.extend(by_id[node_id].depends_on)

233	    bodies: dict[str, set[str]] = {}

238	        if entry is None:

240	        if entry.kind != "task":

242	        body = _collect_loop_body(by_id, entry.id)
243	        if node.id in body:

247	        judge = by_id.get(node.condition)

252	        if judge.id not in body:

284	        visiting.remove(node_id)
285	        visited.add(node_id)
286	
287	    for node_id in graph:

374	    def _insert_execution(
375	        self,
376	        execution_id: str,
377	        workflow_id: str,
378	        input_data: dict[str, Any],
379	        timeout: float | None,
380	        subscriptions: list[dict[str, Any]] | None,
381	        tenant: str = DEFAULT_TENANT,
382	    ) -> dict[str, Any]:
383	        """Insert a running execution and its start event; caller holds a transaction."""
384	        workflow_row = self.store.connection.execute(
385	            "SELECT document FROM workflows WHERE tenant = ? AND id = ?",
386	            (tenant, workflow_id),
387	        ).fetchone()
388	        if not workflow_row:
389	            raise NotFoundError(f"workflow {workflow_id} was not found")
390	        workflow = Workflow.parse(self.store.decode(workflow_row["document"]))
391	        # A duplicate identifier does not grow the holding, so it keeps the
392	        # ordinary identifier conflict even when the tenant is at quota.
393	        existing = self.store.connection.execute(
394	            "SELECT 1 FROM executions WHERE tenant = ? AND id = ?",
395	            (tenant, execution_id),
396	        ).fetchone()
397	        if existing:
398	            raise ConflictError(f"execution {execution_id} already exists")
399	        self._assert_within_quota(tenant, "executions")
400	        loops = {node.id: _new_loop_state() for node in workflow.nodes if node.kind == "loop"}
401	        has_approvals = any(node.approval is not None for node in workflow.nodes)
402	        deadline = time.time() + timeout if timeout is not None else None
403	        state = {
404	            "id": execution_id,
405	            "workflow_id": workflow_id,
406	            "status": "running",
407	            "termination_reason": None,
408	            "timeout_seconds": timeout,
409	            "deadline_at": deadline,
410	            "input": input_data,
411	            "completed_nodes": [],
412	            "skipped_nodes": [],
413	            "failed_nodes": [],
414	            "condition_results": {},
415	            "outputs": {},
416	            "attempts": {},
417	            "loops": loops,
418	        }
419	        # Approval state exists only for workflows that declare approval
420	        # points, so every other execution keeps its baseline state shape.
421	        if has_approvals:
422	            state["waiting_approval"] = None
423	            state["approvals"] = []
424	        try:
425	            self.store.connection.execute(
426	                "INSERT INTO executions(tenant, id, workflow_id, state) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)",
427	                (tenant, execution_id, workflow_id, self.store.encode(state)),
428	            )
429	        except Exception as error:
430	            if "UNIQUE constraint" in str(error):
431	                raise ConflictError(f"execution {execution_id} already exists") from error
432	            raise
433	        for position, subscription in enumerate(subscriptions or []):
434	            self.store.connection.execute(
435	                "INSERT INTO subscriptions(tenant, owner_type, owner_id, position, document) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)",
436	                (tenant, "execution", execution_id, position, self.store.encode(subscription)),
437	            )
438	        started_payload: dict[str, Any] = {
439	            "workflow_id": workflow_id,
440	            "input": input_data,
441	            "loops": loops,
442	            "timeout_seconds": timeout,
443	            "deadline_at": deadline,
444	        }
445	        if has_approvals:
446	            started_payload["waiting_approval"] = None
447	            started_payload["approvals"] = []
448	        self._append(
449	            execution_id,
450	            "execution_started",
451	            started_payload,
452	            tenant,
453	        )
454	        return state
